\chapter{Where You Are From}
\label{ch:te-where-you-are-from}
\hlchaptermodality{77}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say which town and country I am from in Telugu, count past twenty, and give my age.}

Complete TE-C77-thirty and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nunci]{\te{నుంచి} (nunci) — from}

\label{lesson:TE-C77-from}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kaṣṭaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{నుంచి}}
\textbf{\te{నుంచి}} (\emph{nunci}) — \textquotedblleft{}from\textquotedblright{}.

You already have \textbf{-\te{కు}}, \textquotedblleft{}to\textquotedblright{}, and \textbf{-\te{లో}}, \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{}. \te{నుంచి} is the third of the set and the one an introduction needs.

Like them it follows its noun: \textbf{\te{గ్రామం} \te{నుంచి}} — \textquotedblleft{}from the village\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the third relation word}]
Three now sit behind a noun and do three different jobs: \textbf{-\te{లో}} puts you inside, \textbf{-\te{కు}} sends you toward, \textbf{\te{నుంచి}} takes you out of. Telugu has no words in front of nouns at all; everything a preposition would do in English is done by a piece glued to the back.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The direction you came out of.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nunci}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nunci}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{grāmaṁ nunci}, then \emph{grāmāniki} — out of, and into
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{eppuḍu vastāru?}, then \emph{snēhituḍu}, then say \emph{nunci}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{నుంచి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}from\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[paṭṭaṇaṁ]{\te{పట్టణం} (paṭṭaṇaṁ) — a town}

\label{lesson:TE-C77-town}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nunci} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{పట్టణం}}
\textbf{\te{పట్టణం}} (\emph{paṭṭaṇaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a town\textquotedblright{}.

You already have \te{గ్రామం}, the village. \te{పట్టణం} is the larger settlement, the one with the shops and the bargaining in it.

\textbf{\te{నేను} \te{పట్టణం} \te{నుంచి}} — \textquotedblleft{}I am from a town.\textquotedblright{} That sentence needs no verb, exactly like \te{నా} \te{పేరు}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Somewhere to be from.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{paṭṭaṇaṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{paṭṭaṇaṁ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{grāmaṁ}, then \emph{paṭṭaṇaṁ}, and say which is bigger
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mundu}, then \emph{koḍuku}, then say \emph{paṭṭaṇaṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{పట్టణం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a town\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dēśaṁ]{\te{దేశం} (dēśaṁ) — a country}

\label{lesson:TE-C77-country}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{paṭṭaṇaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{దేశం}}
\textbf{\te{దేశం}} (\emph{dēśaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a country\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit tatsama, and the same word behind Hindi \emph{desh}. It scales the ladder up once more: \te{గ్రామం}, \te{పట్టణం}, \te{దేశం}.

\textbf{\te{ఏ} \te{దేశం}?} — \textquotedblleft{}which country?\textquotedblright{} is a question you will be asked in the first minute of any exam interview.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The largest place you can be from.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dēśaṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dēśaṁ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{grāmaṁ}, \emph{paṭṭaṇaṁ}, \emph{dēśaṁ}, smallest to largest
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{saṁvatsaraṁ}, then \emph{kūturu}, then say \emph{dēśaṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{దేశం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a country\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Bhāratadēśaṁ]{\te{భారతదేశం} (Bhāratadēśaṁ) — India}

\label{lesson:TE-C77-india}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{dēśaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{భారతదేశం}}
\textbf{\te{భారతదేశం}} (\emph{Bhāratadēśaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}India\textquotedblright{}.

Your first Telugu proper name, and you can already read half of it: \textbf{\te{భారత}} plus the \te{దేశం} you learned a moment ago.

\textbf{\te{నేను} \te{భారతదేశం} \te{నుంచి}} — \textquotedblleft{}I am from India.\textquotedblright{} Swap in the name of wherever you are actually from and the sentence still works.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A place with a name, in a sentence that says you came from it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{Bhāratadēśaṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{Bhāratadēśaṁ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{nēnu Bhāratadēśaṁ nunci}, then say it with your own country instead
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{cālā manci}, then \emph{cevi}, then say \emph{Bhāratadēśaṁ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{భారతదేశం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}India\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[muppai]{\te{ముప్పై} (muppai) — thirty (and the tens above it)}

\label{lesson:TE-C77-thirty}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{Bhāratadēśaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ముప్పై}}
\textbf{\te{ముప్పై}} (\emph{muppai}) — \textquotedblleft{}thirty\textquotedblright{}.

Your counting stopped at \te{ఇరవై}, twenty. The tens above it are built the same way, from the units you already know:

\te{ముప్పై} 30, \textbf{\te{నలభై}} 40, \textbf{\te{యాభై}} 50, \textbf{\te{అరవై}} 60, \textbf{\te{డెబ్బై}} 70, \textbf{\te{ఎనభై}} 80, \textbf{\te{తొంభై}} 90, \textbf{\te{వంద}} 100. Every one but \te{వంద} ends in the same \textbf{-\te{ై}} twenty does.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: an age, at last}]
You have long been able to ask \textbf{\te{నీ} \te{వయసెంత}?} and unable to answer it, because the numbers stopped at twenty and no word for a year existed. With the tens and with \te{సంవత్సరం}, the answer is now sayable: \textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{ముప్పై} \te{సంవత్సరాలు}} — \textquotedblleft{}I am thirty\textquotedblright{}, literally \textquotedblleft{}to me, thirty years\textquotedblright{}. Note the dative \te{నాకు}: an age is something that has arrived at you, like every other Telugu experience.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Numbers past twenty: an age, a price, a year.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{muppai}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{muppai}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} count the tens aloud: \emph{iravai}, \emph{muppai}, \emph{nalabhai}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ceḍḍa}, then \emph{kannu}, then say \emph{muppai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ముప్పై} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}thirty (and the tens above it)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
